To tip or turn over.
d.x: When he upended the bottle of water over his sleeping sister, the lid popped off and surprised them both.

d.g: To destroy, invalidate, overthrow, or defeat.
d.x: The scientific evidence upended the popular myth.

d.g: To affect or upset drastically.
d.x: By the middle of March 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic upended normal life for virtually all Americans.

upend.e: English up- English end English upend From up- + end.

d.g: To heave or lift up; raise up or aloft.
To lift or thrust something upward forcefully, or be similarly lifted or thrust upward.
To be lifted up; rise.

upheave.e: From Middle English upheven, from Old English ūpāhebban (“to lift up, raise up, exalt, rise in the air, fly”), equivalent to up- + heave. Cognate with Dutch opheffen (“to lift, raise”), German aufheben (“to lift, raise, cancel, repeal”).

d.g: To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.
d.x: The mournful train/ Echoed her grief, [...]/ With groans, and hands upheld, to move his mind, /Besought his pity to their helpless kind

d.g: To keep erect; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling
d.x: A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.

d.g: To support by approval or encouragement; to vindicate; to confirm (something which has been questioned)
d.x: let any moral come along and she would uphold it

uphold.e: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold. Compare Dutch ophouden (“to stop, cease, hold up”), German aufhalten (“to stop, halt, detain”). Compare also Middle Low German upholt, Old Norse upphald (“uphold, support”).

d.g: To fit padding, stuffing, springs, webbing and fabric covering to (furniture).

upholster.e: Back-formation from upholsterer (“tradesman who finishes furniture”), from Middle English upholdester, variant of Middle English upholder (“dealer in small goods”), from upholden (“to repair, uphold”); equivalent to uphold + -ster. …

d.g: To transfer data to a computer on a network, especially to a server on the Internet.
d.x: You will have to convert your photograph to a jpg format if you wish to upload it.

d.g: To transfer jurisdiction and responsibility of a government asset or service to a higher level of government.
d.x: Our government will not be uploading the DVP or Gardiner Expressway and will not be imposing any new tolls on any roads in Ontario.

d.g: Such a file transfer.

upload.e: English up- English load English upload From up- + load.

d.g: cause to become alive again

upraise.e: English up- English raise English upraise From up- + raise.

d.g: To rebel or revolt; to take part in an uprising.
d.x: They had decided to uprise rather than face punishment, and they wanted all the help they could get.

d.g: The act of rising; appearance above the horizon; rising.

uprise.e: From Middle English uprisen, from Old English ūprīsan (“to rise up”), equivalent to up- + rise. Cognate with Icelandic upprisa (“resurrection”), Middle Low German oprīsinge (“uprising”). Compare also Icelandic uppreisn (“an uprising, revolt”).

d.g: To tear up (a plant, etc.) by the roots, or as if by the roots; to extirpate, to root up.
d.x: Thou shakest the earth with the thunder of thy terror, and uprootest the huge oaks on the highest hills with the echo of thy voice.

d.g: To destroy (something) utterly; to eradicate, exterminate.
d.x: [B]ravely bearing on, thy will / Is destined an eternal war to wage / With tyranny and falshood, and uproot / The germs of misery from the human heart.

d.g: To remove (someone or something) from a familiar circumstance, especially suddenly and unwillingly.
Of oneself or someone: to move away from a familiar environment (for example, to live elsewhere).

uproot.e: PIE word *wréh₂ds From up- (prefix indicating a higher direction or position) + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place; to eradicate, exterminate”, verb). …
